title: The hiding place
hookLine: the ten Boom family, Dutch watchmakers, hide Jews in a secret room; Corrie later forgives a guard

lines: A WALL IN THE WRONG PLACE.
cards: Clocks tick along the walls of a narrow house in Haarlem, in the Netherlands. Downstairs is the family watch shop.
Upstairs, at the top of a steep staircase, is a small bedroom, and at the back of it is a wall that isn't quite where it should be.

Behind it is a space barely deep enough for people to stand in a row, with a little vent for air. When the buzzer sounds, the people living in the house have a short time to climb in, close the panel, and be silent.

teach.b: The ten Booms were Dutch Reformed Christians, an old watchmaker, Casper, and his grown daughters Betsie and Corrie, who opened their home to Jews and members of the resistance when the Nazis occupied their country.
The secret room was built behind a false wall in Corrie's bedroom. Then someone betrayed them. Police raided the house and arrested the family.
They never found the room, and the people hiding inside it got out alive. The ten Booms were not so fortunate. Casper died after a short time in prison.

Corrie and Betsie were sent to the women's camp at Ravensbrück, and Betsie died there. Corrie was released, and after the war she traveled and told the story, and later told it in a book, The Hiding Place.
In the King James Bible: "Thou art my hiding place and my shield: I hope in thy word." A family hid people, and trusted that they themselves were hidden in God. Then the harder part.
After speaking at a church in Germany about forgiveness, Corrie saw a man coming toward her with his hand out. She recognized him as a guard from Ravensbrück.
By her own telling, she couldn't lift her hand. She felt nothing warm toward him. She prayed for help, took his hand, and only then, she said, did the feeling come.
She didn't describe forgiveness as forgetting, or as saying it didn't matter, but as an act she chose before she could feel it, with help from beyond herself.
Her story is often told in churches, and some readers gently add that no one should be rushed into that handshake.

how: The ten Boom house in Haarlem is now a museum where visitors can see the hiding place, and Corrie ten Boom's story of forgiving a guard is often told in churches, especially among evangelical Christians.

games.q: you're Corrie, after a talk on forgiveness. a former guard from your camp walks up with his hand out. what happens?
o: she walks away without a word.
she feels nothing, prays for help, and takes his hand.
she shakes it at once and feels only warmth.
games.why: by her own telling, she couldn't lift her hand. she prayed, took it, and only then did the feeling come.

practice: Go gently. Bring to mind something someone did that you've never let go of, not the worst thing unless you're ready, and notice how your hand feels: clenched, maybe.
You don't have to forgive it today; Corrie's way was to ask for help before the feeling came. If you pray, ask for that help; if not, open your hand on your knee and hold it open.
